definition: The set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to make predictions on inputs it hasn't specifically seen before.
details: Inductive bias is built into model architecture choices — for example, convolutional networks assume spatial locality matters, while transformers make comparatively fewer built-in assumptions about input structure, relying more on data to learn such patterns.
story: Picture guardrails on a mountain road — not there to slow you down on the straightaways, but to keep you from flying off the cliff. Boil it down and it is this: The set of assumptions a learning algorithm uses to make predictions on inputs it hasn't specifically seen before. Here is why it matters: Inductive bias is built into model architecture choices — for example, convolutional networks assume spatial locality matters, while transformers make comparatively fewer built-in assumptions about input structure, relying more on data to learn such patterns. It is the difference between “it works” and “it is safe to put in front of people.” That deliberate caution is Inductive Bias.
